title: third-party-api-rate-limits-failure-mode-sla-exhibit
content:
Purpose
This exhibit is intended to be attached to third-party integration agreements (trial, sandbox, or production) where Redwood systems (or Redwood customers) rely on an external API for inference, telemetry, or model artifacts. It captures the operational expectations for rate limiting, error modes, and remedial obligations. Use this as an exhibit to a Master Services Agreement or as a standalone schedule for shorter eval contracts.

Summary of intent (plain language)
- Protect Redwood customers from silent degradation when a vendor enforces limits or experiences failure.
- Define observable signals, expected behaviors, and mitigation/fallback requirements.
- Provide a transparent escalation path and a clear credit/termination framework tied to objective metrics.

Key definitions
- Consumer: Redwood or Redwood customer making API calls to the Vendor.
- Vendor: third party providing the API/service.
- Rate limit event: vendor-imposed request throttling that results in 429 or equivalent for >=1% of calls over a rolling 15-minute window.
- Degraded availability: vendor responses with 5xx errors, timeouts, or >50% increased p95 latency relative to baseline, sustained for at least 30 minutes.
- Emergency throttle: vendor-initiated limiting due to capacity, attack, or misconfiguration that affects production traffic.

1) Rate limiting behavior and transparency
1.1 Rate limit types: Vendor will only apply the following kinds of rate limits: per-tenant qps, per-IP qps, and per-token concurrency limits. Bursty client behavior should be tolerated up to a well-documented burst window (e.g., 2x sustained rate for up to 30s).
1.2 Response headers: On every response the Vendor will include machine-readable headers: X-Vendor-RateLimit-Limit, X-Vendor-RateLimit-Remaining, X-Vendor-RateLimit-Reset, and X-Vendor-Response-Id. For throttled requests, X-Vendor-Retry-After is required and must be in seconds.
1.3 Programmatic notice: For any persistent rate limit change that affects >=5% of synced customers, Vendor will publish a programmatic notice via the agreed webhook (or email and API portal) at least 24 hours in advance and will provide a JSON changelog of the new limits.
1.4 Grace and adaptive back-off: Vendor must accept standard exponential backoff with jitter. 429 responses should be treated as transient for up to 3 retries per request by the Redeeming party; vendor must support idempotency where feasible and document when retries may cause side-effects.

2) Failure modes, signals, and expected vendor actions
2.1 Observable signals: Vendor should emit and make available via the operational portal the following metrics per tenant: total calls, 2xx/4xx/5xx counts, p50/p95/p99 latency, active connections, and rate-limit events. A stream or a 1-minute granularity export is preferred for incident analysis.
2.2 Degraded availability playbook: On detection of degraded availability (as defined above), Vendor shall: (a) notify Redwood via the escalation channel within 5 minutes, (b) publish incident status to the status page and operational webhook, (c) provide a rolling 15-minute summary of impact and mitigation steps until service is restored.
2.3 Emergency throttle: If an emergency throttle is required, Vendor must (i) attempt targeted throttling (by tenant or API key) rather than global shutdown, (ii) provide immediate telemetry showing traffic segments affected, and (iii) enable temporary quota increases by mutual agreement for high-priority customers.

3) Fallback, retry semantics, and graceful degradation requirements
3.1 Graceful fallback requirement: Redwood (or its customers) must be able to detect vendor throttling/failure and automatically fall back to one of the following strategies: cached responses, degraded but allowable default content, best-effort local model, or queued background retry. Vendor must document eventual consistency and staleness guarantees for cached artifacts used as fallbacks.
3.2 Data semantics during retries: Vendor must document exactly which operations are idempotent. For non-idempotent operations, Vendor shall provide a replay-id or server-generated operation idempotency-key in the response to help clients avoid duplicates.

4) Metrics, reporting, and monthly guarantees
4.1 Availability guarantee: Vendor shall maintain a monthly availability of 99.9% for API endpoints defined in Appendix A (unless alternate endpoints are marked as beta). Availability measured as (successful requests / total requests) excluding maintenance windows and agreed customer-side misconfiguration.
4.2 Rate limit transparency: Monthly report will include per-tenant rate limit events, median retry counts observed by Redwood, and any policy changes.
4.3 SLA credits: If availability falls below 99.9% but >=99.0% in a billing month, Vendor will credit 5% of the monthly service fee pro rata. If availability <99.0%, credit equals 20% unless remedial actions agreed. Credits are Redwood's sole monetary remedy; non-monetary remedies (priority support, remediation plans) will be negotiated for recurring violations.

5) Evidence and auditability
5.1 Logs and evidence: On request, Vendor will provide a 30-day export of request logs, rate-limit events, and incident timelines for the impacted tenant(s) in a mutually agreed JSON/CSV schema. Sensitive payloads may be redacted, but metadata sufficient for debugging (timestamps, request ids, API paths, response codes, headers) must be provided.
5.2 Audit period: For critical incidents impacting >=10% of calls across Redwood customers, Vendor will participate in a joint post-incident review within 14 days and provide root-cause analysis and remediation roadmap for 90 days following the incident.

6) Security and abuse controls
6.1 Abuse mitigation: Vendor must have DDoS and abuse mitigation controls and document expected false-positive rates, escalation thresholds, and manual override procedures.
6.2 Credential compromise: In the event of suspected API key compromise that leads to abusive traffic, Vendor will: rotate affected keys within 2 hours of confirmation, notify impacted tenants, and provide logs for the compromised window.

7) Termination and temporary suspension
7.1 Short-term emergency suspension: Vendor may temporarily suspend access to a tenant for immediate security reasons but must notify Redwood and the customer within 30 minutes and provide an expected restoration ETA. Suspension should be targeted and narrowly scoped.
7.2 Termination for repeated degradation: If Vendor records three (3) distinct months within any 12-month period where availability <99.0% or repeated unannounced throttles occur, Redwood may terminate the integration with 30 days notice and without penalty.

Negotiation notes / redlines to consider (internal)
- 24-hour programmatic notice for any persistent limit change is strict; vendors will push back. Alternative: require 72-hour notice for >10% change and immediate programmatic change-log for emergency ops. (JIRA: SEC-1423)
- SLA credit ceilings — confirm alignment with commercial finance (CN-908) for small vendors.
- Audit log export cadence: 30 days retention might be insufficient for some customers; consider higher-tier retention as an add-on.

Appendix A: API endpoint categorization (placeholder)
- production-inference.redwood.vendor/v1/generate (expected availability SLA)
- production-embeddings.redwood.vendor/v1/encode (expected availability SLA)
- admin/health and admin/metrics endpoints (operational, not customer-facing)

Open questions / TODOs
- Decide whether to enforce per-tenant burst windows or allow vendor-managed burst policing (ask vendors for historical burst tolerances).
- Add a sample webhook schema for programmatic notices (owner: Jordan Meyer).
- Confirm whether credits are cumulative with other contractual remedies (legal).

Quick negotiation script (for partner managers)
- Emphasize transparency: the headers and programmatic notice requirements reduce ops load on both sides.
- Offer optional paid higher-tier SLAs (longer retention, guaranteed priority scaling) to keep baseline concession-friendly.
- For early-stage vendors, propose a 6-month pilot with limited SLA credit exposure and a joint runbook pilot.

Notes to self
- Align with product: check Hosted API fallback recommendations with eng/product (ticket: PRO-775).
- Add sample JSON of rate-limit headers and webhook payload in the next version.
